blocks.text: “Please put all fifty boxes in the partly ruined building attached to the house. It is marked ‘A’ on the rough plan included with this letter. Your agent will easily recognise the place. It is the house’s ancient chapel. The goods leave on the train at 9:30 tonight. They are due at King’s Cross at 4:30 tomorrow afternoon. Our client wants them delivered as soon as possible. Please have teams of horses ready at King’s Cross at that time. Then take the goods straight to their destination. We want to avoid any delays caused by your departments’ usual rules about payment. We therefore include a cheque for ten pounds (£10). Please confirm that you have received it. If the cost is less, you can return the money left over. If it is more, please tell us. We will immediately send a cheque for the extra amount. When you leave, put the keys in the house’s main hall. The owner can collect them there when he enters with his own copy of the key.
“We are urging you in every way to work as quickly as possible. Please do not think we are being less polite than business requires.
“We are, dear Sirs, “Faithfully yours, “Samuel F. Billington & Son.”
Letter, Messrs. Carter, Paterson & Co., London, to Messrs. Billington & Son, Whitby.

“We confirm that we have received £10. We return a cheque for £1 17s. 9d, the amount left over. The bill included with this letter shows this amount and confirms payment. The goods have been delivered exactly as you instructed. The keys were left in a parcel in the main hall, as directed.
“We are, dear Sirs, “Yours respectfully. “On behalf of Carter, Paterson & Co.”

18 August.—I am happy today. I am sitting on the seat in the churchyard as I write. Lucy is so much better. Last night she slept well all night and did not disturb me once. The colour of roses already seems to be returning to her cheeks. Still, she looks terribly pale and weak. If she had too few healthy red blood cells, I could understand it. But she does not. She is happy and full of life and good cheer. Her unhealthy unwillingness to talk seems to have passed completely. She has just reminded me of that night, as if I needed reminding. She reminded me that I found her asleep here, on this very seat. As she spoke, she playfully tapped her boot’s heel on the flat stone and said:—

“My poor little feet didn’t make much noise then! I suppose poor old Mr. Swales would have said why. He would have told me I didn’t want to wake up Geordie.” She was so willing to talk that I asked about her dreams. Had she dreamed at all that night? Before she answered, her forehead gathered into that sweet little frown. Arthur says he loves that look. I call him Arthur because she always does. And really, I am not surprised that he loves it. Then she continued, speaking almost as if she were dreaming. She seemed to be trying to remember it herself:—

“It wasn’t quite a dream, but it all seemed real. All I wanted was to be here, in this spot. I don’t know why, because I was afraid of something. I don’t know what. I remember going through the streets and over the bridge. Yet I suppose I was asleep. A fish jumped as I passed, and I leaned over to look at it. As I went up the steps, I heard many dogs howling. It seemed the whole town must be full of dogs, all howling at once. Then I had an unclear memory of something long and dark, with red eyes. It was just like what we saw in the sunset. Something very sweet and very bitter was all around me at once. Then I seemed to be sinking into deep green water. There was a singing sound in my ears. I have heard that drowning men hear such a sound. Then everything seemed to be slipping away from me. My soul seemed to leave my body and float about in the air. I seem to remember that the West Lighthouse was right below me at one point. Then there was a terrible, unbearable feeling, as if I were in an earthquake. I came back and found you shaking my body. I saw you doing it before I felt you.”
